articles.title_orig: More Americans pay this Obama-era investment tax every year — how to avoid it
articles.title_zh: More Americans pay this Obama-era investment tax every year — how to avoid it
articles.content_orig:
Every year, more Americans pay an extra tax levy on their investment gains — but there's still time to reduce or avoid that bill for 2026, experts say.
Net investment income tax , or NIIT, is a 3.8% levy on investment income once earnings exceed $200,000 for single filers or $250,000 for married couples filing jointly. The tax was enacted in 2010 under President Barack Obama to help fund healthcare via the Affordable Care Act .
Unlike the federal income tax or capital gains brackets , the NIIT earnings limits don't adjust annually for inflation.
As a result, "more clients get hit every year," said certified financial planner Michael Walstedt, founding advisor of Reliant Wealth Advisory in Hoboken, New Jersey.
Roughly 5.6% of tax returns included NIIT for 2025, according to IRS data released in November for returns processed through mid-July 2026. That's up from about 3.7% for the same time frame in 2021.
As more investors pay NIIT, here are some key things to know.
NIIT applies when you have investment income and your earnings exceed the modified adjusted gross income, or MAGI, limits, according to certified financial planner Marianela Collado , CEO of Tobias Financial Advisors in Plantation, Florida.
"The trick is to keep an eye on both of these numbers," said Collado, who is also a certified public accountant and member of CNBC's Financial Advisor Council .
For the NIIT earnings limit, MAGI is typically the same as adjusted gross income , or AGI. One exception would be if you have foreign income, which changes the calculation. You can find last year's AGI on line 11a of your 2025 tax return .
MAGI limits by filing status
Married filing jointly: $250,000
Married filing separately: $125,000
Head of household (with qualifying person): $200,000
Qualifying widow(er) with dependent child: $250,000
NIIT applies to investment income, which includes interest, dividends, annuities, royalties, certain rents, and more. It can also include capital gains from a primary home sale , for profits that exceed the IRS exclusions. The exclusion is $250,000 for single filers or $500,000 for married couples.
The levy stacks on top of regular income tax rates, or capital gains tax — which can be 0%, 15% or 20%, depending on earnings. That means higher earners can pay up to 23.8% on investment income, including long-term capital gains and NIIT.
The NIIT calculation is 3.8% multiplied by the lesser of:
For example, if your MAGI is $30,000 above the NIIT earnings limit and you have $100,000 of investment income, you would pay 3.8% of $30,000, or $1,140.
Alternatively, if your MAGI is $120,000 above the threshold and you have $100,000 of investment income, you would owe 3.8% of $100,000, or $3,800.
As year-end approaches, investors should run projections to estimate their adjusted gross income, which can impact NIIT, among other tax consequences, experts say.
If you're above the NIIT limits, you could reduce AGI by boosting pretax 401(k) deferrals or health savings account contributions, according to Collado with Tobias Financial Advisors.
While employee 401(k) deferrals must happen by Dec. 31, you have until next year's tax deadline for health savings account contributions for 2026.
You might also try to avoid selling assets before year-end, which could further boost AGI, experts say. Of course, any current-year tax moves should consider your long-term financial goals.
Amid recent stock market volatility , investors may also consider so-called tax-loss harvesting , which uses losses to offset other portfolio gains, Walstedt with Reliant Wealth Advisory said.
If your losses exceed profits, you can subtract up to $3,000 from regular income. After that, you can carry remaining losses into future tax years.
However, if you're planning to reinvest the sale proceeds, you need to know the " wash sale rule ," which blocks the tax-loss harvesting tax break for buying a "substantially identical" asset within 30 days before or after the sale.

Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas has extended his contract with the ⁠chip designer to lead the company through 2033, confirming his ​leadership role ​at the ​firm amid speculation that Nvidia could tap him for the top job after Jensen Huang's resignation.
Nvidia's board ⁠had ‌approached Haas in its search ⁠for a successor to Huang, the Financial Times reported earlier this month, following Huang's exit amid revelations of extramarital affairs ‌including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Analysts had also pointed to Haas ​as a solid candidate for the CEO role at Nvidia, given he spent his formative years at the company, rising to ⁠vice president and general manager of its computing products ‌business, before joining Arm in ‌2013.
Haas became the British chipmaker's chief executive in 2022 and oversaw its return to public markets ⁠through a $65 billion Nasdaq listing the following year.
Arm licenses ⁠processor designs used across smartphones, ⁠PCs, servers and connected devices.
"I've never been more confident about Arm's future... I'm wholly ​committed to realizing ‌Arm's full potential for many years to come," Haas said in a statement on Monday.
Haas will also assume the role of vice chairman of ​SoftBank Group , effective December 1, Arm ‌Holdings said on Monday.

articles.title_orig: A battered stock market looks for the bottom: What to watch this week
articles.title_zh: A battered stock market looks for the bottom: What to watch this week
articles.content_orig:
By HUGO DUNCAN, BUSINESS EDITOR
Updated: 09:37 EST, 23 November 2026
As stock market debuts go, it certainly lived up to the hype.
Anthropic shares soared by nearly 40 per cent in the first minutes of trading in New York last Thursday – giving it a value of more than $2trillion.
Its seven founders, all in their 30s and 40s, including Brighton-born Jack Clark, were sitting on fortunes of $26billion each. Thousands more staff were millionaires many times over.
So, was the blockbuster float the tonic Wall Street needed after weeks of market turmoil?
The AI developer, best known for its Claude chatbot, surrendered early gains though still ended its first session of trading up 17 per cent. On Friday, it crashed back to the $83 listing price before closing at $88.91, down 8.5 per cent.
More worrying still, trading screens were a sea of red from east to west, with the MSCI All Country World Index, a key benchmark of global stocks, suffering its longest losing streak for three years.
Once again, it was technology stocks that bore the brunt of the sell-off, with New York’s blue-chip Nasdaq 100 index now down by more than 18 per cent from its peak a little over a month ago.
Traders on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on Friday morning, after AI developer Anthropic debuted on the stock market. It crashed back to its $83 listing price before closing at $88.91, down 8.5 per cent
Among the AI pioneers that had led the charge earlier in the year – the hyperscalers, the neoclouds, the data centre developers – it was carnage.
Since reaching record highs in recent months, CoreWeave, SanDisk and Nebius are down some 70 per cent, while Intel and Oracle have fallen around 60 per cent. The list goes on.
Nvidia – the posterchild of the AI revolution that was left reeling from the sudden departure of rockstar boss Jensen Huang over a string of affairs before his dramatic reinstatement on Monday – was down more than 40 per cent in a rout that wiped around $2.5trillion off the value of what was once the world’s biggest company.
Nvidia shares bounced back after on Monday as investors welcomed his return. Tech stocks also rallied - but the outlook remains deeply uncertain.
‘We’re already in a stealth bear market,’ notes one Mayfair-based hedge fund manager. This refers to a market in which a specific sector falls 20 per cent or more from its peak.
The big question before Anthropic’s record-breaking initial public offering (IPO) was whether it would be enough to save the AI trade and restore faith in the stuttering stock market.
The answer was a resounding no – and many of the world’s top investors are fearful of what comes next.
They are not alone. Wall Street’s so-called ‘fear index’ – the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) – is at its highest level since March, when markets were shuddering at the sound of Donald Trump’s war on Iran.
‘A week from hell,’ is how Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, referred to last week.
‘It’s gritty out there,’ says a respected City fund manager who looks after hundreds of millions of pounds of savings. ‘People have ploughed headlong into the US without thinking about valuation. There’s a period of adjustment ahead. We’ll have to see how long and how bad it is.’
For two of America’s most prominent investors – Ray Dalio, founder of the world’s biggest hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, and Ken Griffin, of rival Citadel – we are in the midst of a bubble that is one day bound to burst.
‘Almost every technology boom creates a bubble, then a bust, whether it’s railroads, the Industrial Revolution or the late 1920s,’ explains Dalio.
Berkshire Hathaway, which was the home of the ‘Oracle of Omaha’ – Warren Buffett – for six decades until he stood down as chairman in September, now holds a staggering $377.4billion in cash.
While this does not necessarily mean he believes a crash is coming, at the very least it shows he does not think many stocks offer good value at their current prices.
Owen Lamont, a fund manager at Acadian Asset Management in Boston and a former University of Chicago finance professor, notes that as recently as January he penned an article titled ‘We are not in an AI bubble’.
‘Today, I would no longer write those words,’ he says. ‘I think there is a 70 per cent chance that as of November 2026 we are already in an AI bubble in the US stock market. The smart money is selling.’
Closer to home, the head of market strategy at one of the City’s leading investment banks is more convinced than ever that the bubble is about to burst, so much so he has sold his own private share holdings.
‘We have consistently warned of an AI bubble since May and have become more bearish,’ says Joachim Klement at Panmure Liberum. ‘We think the AI bubble is about to burst. Market dynamics have turned decisively bearish.’
The trigger for his own decision to sell – and move money into government bonds – was the S&P 500 moving below a key threshold known as the 200-day moving average.
‘I know I will be out of stocks when the AI bubble bursts,’ he says.
‘Almost every technology boom creates a bubble, then a bust, whether it’s railroads, the Industrial Revolution or the late 1920s,’ explains Ray Dalio, founder of the world’s biggest hedge fund Bridgewater Associates
Gary Channon, a fund manager at Phoenix Asset Management in London, is similarly pessimistic. He says: 'The current bubble has almost run its course. It has been a great ride, but the building is on fire, save yourselves.’
Whether or not a crash is coming, one thing is for sure, according to one of London’s leading fund managers: ‘A lot of people have already been very badly burned.’
He explains: ‘In the first half of this year, there has been a lot of FOMO in the market, or fear of missing out, with a lot of unsophisticated investors going into AI. The last few months have been very painful for them.’
A crash would spell misery for millions of British savers with money tied up in shares through their pensions, stocks and shares Isas and other investments.
The London stock market – with its banks, oil majors and pharmaceutical groups, but very few tech stocks – has fared better than its US counterparts in the recent turmoil.
On November 16, the FTSE 100 came within a whisker of a new record close. The mood has darkened since then however, as storm clouds drift over the Atlantic, and London’s premier shares index racked up losses of 5 per cent in just five days last week.
Panmure’s Klement believes ‘UK stocks are the best hiding place’ from the turmoil – identifying companies from GSK and AstraZeneca to Greggs and Wetherspoon.
‘After all, if the market crashes, what else can you do but go to a pub?’ he notes ruefully, adding that, in fact, ‘the best positions to take are cash and the foetal position’.
Such is the might of US tech, the bursting of the AI bubble could drag global markets down with it.
And it is not just Wall Street that is suffering.
Asian shares clocked up their worst week since 2020. Japan’s Nikkei 225 and South Korea’s Kospi tumbled 5 per cent on Friday alone, while Taiwanese shares were down 17 per cent in their biggest weekly decline since 1990.
There has been no shortage of warnings from global regulators, with almost every financial enforcer on Earth sounding the alarm, from the International Monetary Fund to the world’s central bank chiefs.
Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey has warned the vast sums borrowed by the AI industry to fund the revolution are now a risk to financial stability.
And Boris Vujcic, vice president at the European Central Bank, has spoken of an ‘abrupt repricing and significant valuation losses’ in stock markets – which sounds a lot like a crash – if investor sentiment about AI suddenly sours.
This could hardly come at a worse time.
The global economy is reeling from an energy price shock – stemming first from Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine and then Trump’s war in Iran – that is squeezing households and businesses alike.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday questioned whether Nvidia's earnings might have been inflated by inappropriate sales to China and urged the company to hire an outsider as CEO.
Why it matters: Nvidia is central to the AI economy, which has been key to U.S. economic growth.
Driving the news: In a Fox News appearance Sunday morning, Bessent said Nvidia owes the market an explanation amid allegations former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy and oversaw sanctions-evading chip sales to Asian companies.
Bessent also said it was "obvious" that some companies doing business with Nvidia were shell companies for Chinese interests and accused the chipmaker of a "culture of noncompliance."
For the record: Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Bessent's remarks.
The intrigue: Huang has been a favorite of President Trump and other administration figures for some time, but Bessent has notably not been as effusive about him as others.
What to watch: Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on Tuesday, its first significant public comments since Huang resigned and CFO Collette Kress took over as acting CEO.

articles.title_orig: AI superintelligence ‘arriving’ warns top Meta executive
articles.title_zh: AI superintelligence ‘arriving’ warns top Meta executive
articles.content_orig:
Meta’s top AI executive has sounded the alarm about the risk of humanity losing control of AI, warning that superintelligence that far exceeds the human intellect is imminent.
Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang issued the warning on Sunday after an employee at AI giant Anthropic announced that he had used Claude to solve the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most difficult problems in mathematics.
Wang said the breakthrough dwarfed any human achievement for “sheer intellectual might”.
The 29-year-old executive said the milestone showed that emerging AI models will be “clearly superhuman” at improving themselves, as well as “massively accelerating” research in fields such as biology, armaments and economics.
“Superintelligence is arriving,” Wang said on X.
“How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in.”
Wang, who co-founded Scale AI before joining Meta as the tech giant’s first chief AI officer last year, said it is unlikely humankind will be able to control AI that achieves unconstrained recursive self-improvement or is “1000x smarter and more capable than humans in every field.”
“Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully,” Wang said.
AI safety advocates have identified recursive self-improvement – where AI models become capable of advancing without human input – as a critical tipping point after which humanity could lose the ability to control the technology.
While the risks of frontier AI have stoked intense debate in Silicon Valley, there is no consensus on how to maximise the benefits of the technology without exposing humanity to catastrophic risks.
Meta has largely positioned itself on the more optimistic side of the debate, with CEO and cofounder Mark Zuckerberg rejecting calls by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for a coordinated slowdown in development to beef up guardrails.
In an essay published in August, Zuckerberg lamented that discussions about AI were “filled with doom” and said the technology should lead to “more people sharing greater prosperity, health and freedom.”
In his post on Sunday, Wang criticised “lazy thinking” within the AI industry that he said treated superintelligence as inevitable.
“We should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI. We should endeavour ourselves to build a technology which delivers a positive future for humanity, where all humans have greater agency and empowerment,” Wang said.
“I strongly believe this is possible, but likely involves the whole industry taking meaningfully different actions from the “default path” in front of us.”

articles.title_orig: China’s Growing Ambitions in Very Low Earth Orbit
articles.title_zh: China’s Growing Ambitions in Very Low Earth Orbit
articles.content_orig:
Join War on the Rocks and gain access to content trusted by policymakers, military leaders, and strategic thinkers worldwide.
A new front in the U.S.-Chinese space race is emerging in the lowest reaches of space : very low Earth orbit, the untapped orbital regime below 320 kilometers. There, China is laying the groundwork for a significant presence, with announced plans for more than 2,200 satellites and an aggressive deployment timeline through 2030.
Chinese satellites at these lower altitudes would allow the People’s Liberation Army to conduct more frequent and detailed surveillance of U.S. forces, and improve Chinese military survivability in conflict. Very low Earth orbit’s denser atmosphere helps protect satellites from debris and nuclear radiation that could disable spacecraft in higher orbits, making China’s space architecture more resilient.
These are strategic advantages the United States should be prepared to counter. The answer is not to match China satellite for satellite, but to improve American space capabilities and survivability. Washington should respond by expanding orbital diversity across its space architecture, assessing where very low Earth orbit offers operational advantages worth pursuing, and working with industry to coordinate the orbit’s development.
As executives at Albedo, a U.S. startup building satellites for very low Earth orbit , we have a stake in the future of this orbital regime. We recognize that the orbit’s advantages come with trade-offs, which we discuss openly below. But our roles have given us a close-up view of its evolution from an experimental frontier into a domain of strategic competition, and we believe China’s ambitions there warrant far more attention in Washington.
Sign Up for Our Newsletter
Satellites operate at vastly different altitudes depending on their missions. At roughly 36,000 kilometers, geostationary Earth orbit keeps satellites over the same region for persistent communications and surveillance. Medium Earth orbit, between roughly 2,000 and 36,000 kilometers, hosts GPS and other navigation satellites. Most new satellite activity is in low Earth orbit , extending to roughly 2,000 kilometers, with most satellites above 450 kilometers. Cheaper to reach than higher orbits, low Earth orbit offers advantages for communications and remote sensing, but is increasingly crowded with satellites and debris. That crowding and the advantages of proximity have drawn both government and commercial interest to very low Earth orbit.
Very low Earth orbit refers to the orbital regime of 320 kilometers and below, where the atmosphere starts to become dense enough to both rapidly clear debris and shield satellites from radiation, benefits that grow stronger as altitude decreases. Since these altitudes lie within the upper atmosphere, drag and atomic oxygen have historically made sustained operations difficult. Though advances in propulsion technology, surface materials, and spacecraft design are now overcoming these challenges, operating so close to Earth still comes with trade-offs. Satellites must expend power thrusting against drag, and while purpose-built designs can support lifespans of around five years , those lifespans can vary as solar activity changes atmospheric density . Another trade-off is coverage: each satellite sees less of Earth , requiring more satellites for broader coverage.
Where proximity to Earth matters, however, very low Earth orbit can bring significant benefits . Remote sensing satellites can achieve substantially higher resolution, helping operators more precisely track military forces on Earth. Proximity also brings stronger communications signals and lower latency, useful for tactical missions at the edge.
Very low Earth orbit also offers distinct resiliency and sustainability advantages. Because the atmosphere is roughly 100 times denser than in higher low Earth orbit, debris that would remain in low Earth orbit for years clears from very low Earth orbit in days to weeks , reducing collision risks for satellites. That same atmosphere provides natural shielding against persistent radiation effects of an orbital nuclear detonation , should one occur during a conflict. This would allow satellites to remain operational even if radiation disrupts those in higher orbits.
The orbit’s economics differ, too. Drag can raise operating and replenishment costs. But smaller, cheaper payloads can match or exceed the performance of larger ones higher up. And for missions requiring protection against nuclear effects, the orbit’s natural shielding avoids hardening costs that would be prohibitively expensive for constellations in higher orbits .
It is these benefits that have made very low Earth orbit a growing priority within China’s space plans. Since 2022, China has successfully operated at least a half-dozen demonstration missions in very low Earth orbit , proving its ability to sustain satellites there. China is now building on those demonstrations with plans to deploy very low Earth orbit constellations at a scale unmatched by any other government.
Publicly announced Chinese plans project more than 2,200 very low Earth orbit satellites, spanning remote sensing, communications, and computing missions. With only about a dozen total satellites operating at these altitudes today, such a buildout would transform very low Earth orbit into a proliferated layer of China’s space infrastructure. The timeline is uncertain, but the trajectory is clear. One senior member of the Chinese Academy of Engineering — the nation’s top engineering academy — recently called the next five years a “critical window” for China in very low Earth orbit , and that the country “must complete the transition from technology experimentation to large-scale application.”
China’s clearest attempt to turn very low Earth orbit into a surveillance layer is the China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation’s Chutian constellation. Announced in 2023, Chutian’s bullet-shaped satellites house many types of remote sensing payloads , with onboard data processing and intersatellite links to coordinate as one network. After at least three successful demonstrations, the company aims for 300 satellites by 2030 and potentially more than 500 thereafter. The constellation is designed to observe any point on Earth as frequently as every 15 minutes — a rate which would allow the People’s Liberation Army to compress its sensor-to-shooter timeline.
The most ambitious plan comes from Hangsheng Satellite, a commercial satellite manufacturer. In August 2026, Hangsheng announced plans to build a 1,920-satellite very low Earth orbit communications and computing constellation . Its plan calls for two demonstrations in 2027, then 24 validation satellites before scaling deployment through 2030 — a demanding manufacturing and launch schedule. But once deployed, the constellation would combine stronger radiofrequency links with very low Earth orbit’s resilience to debris and persistent nuclear radiation, creating a more survivable communications and computing layer. In a conflict that disrupted low Earth orbit, such an architecture could give the Chinese military another layer through which to process, fuse, and distribute information.
Chinese startups are also pursuing very low Earth orbit. In December 2024, AIRSAT, a spin-out of the state-run Aerospace Information Research Institute, launched Haishao-1, China’s first very low Earth orbit synthetic aperture radar satellite . Operating as low as 300 kilometers, its orbit concentrates coverage on the South China Sea and Taiwan, enabling up to 5.7 times more daily observations of the region than current Chinese synthetic aperture radar satellites. Another startup, C-Space, is developing a 48-satellite imagery constellation , alongside communications and navigation capabilities .
China is also coordinating its ambitions through a very low Earth orbit industry alliance chaired by the Chinese Academy of Sci

articles.title_orig: China reiterates stance on US export controls after Trump’s chip remarks
articles.title_zh: China reiterates stance on US export controls after Trump’s chip remarks
articles.content_orig:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”
In September, the European Union unveiled its vision for Canada to become an “associate member” of the bloc. During an E.U.-Canada summit in Montreal in October, the two sides underscored their commitment to this plan, paving the way for deeper cooperation in areas including A

articles.title_zh: Zelenskyy says Ukraine behind drone attacks on Russian ships near Libya
articles.content_orig:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukrainian forces sank ⁠a Russian warship off the coast of Libya, hailing an “exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war”.
Zelenskyy said in a statement on Monday that Ukrainian forces also hit a Russian dry ⁠cargo ship, which he said Russia used to transport weapons.
Zelenskyy said the Merkury, one of Russia’s newest warships, sank after Ukrainian forces launched seven naval drones on Sunday. A KA-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed in the attack, he said.
He confirmed that Ukraine’s forces also attacked the MV Angara, a cargo ship . Libya’s eastern health ministry said that all crew members had been rescued and were receiving treatment.
Authorities in eastern Libya said in a statement that the ship was docked in the port when the explosion occurred.
“The ship was en route back to Russia and its stop was for refuelling and resupply. It is suspected that the ship was attacked by drones”.
The United Nations has called for an independent investigation into Sunday’s drone attacks .
On Monday, the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”.
“Libya cannot afford and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts,” UNSMIL wrote on X.
The eastern administration did not identify who was behind Sunday’s attack but said Libya was “not a party to the Russian-Ukrainian war”.
The oil-rich nation of Libya has been divided between the government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east since the overthrow of longtime ruler Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

articles.title_orig: Hu Bo: Three Major Misunderstandings of China's Claims & Policies in South China Sea
articles.title_zh: Hu Bo: Three Major Misunderstandings of China's Claims & Policies in South China Sea
articles.content_orig:
Hu Bo , Director of the South China Sea Strategic Situation Probing Initiative (SCSPI) and Research Professor and Director of the Centre for Maritime Strategy Studies at Peking University, has argued that Beijing seeks to maintain rather than change the status quo in the South China Sea, and that every step taken by Beijing was a response to the Philippines.
The following is the transcript of Hu’s presentation at the 2026 Manila Dialogue on the South China Sea on November 17, 2026.
The video of Hu’s remarks is also available on SCSPI’s official YouTube channel. The transcript is based on this recording and has been lightly edited for clarity, with Hu's collaboration.
In these two days, we have heard a lot of China’s threat and China’s bullying. So let me tell you a different story.
Before we start, I think we should know that we are living in the international sovereignty system. International relation process is the circle of action and reaction. I would like to share three misunderstandings on China’s claims and China’s policies in the South China Sea.
The dash line, or the nine-dash line, just defines the scope of China’s claims in the South China Sea. It is not the legal basis for China’s claims.
If you notice China’s official statements, you will see that we have four kinds of claims.
The first claim is that China has sovereignty over four island groups including Paracel Islands and Spratly Islands and others, and this kind of sovereignty is based on international practice and the UN Charter. Many have been talking about distance, but distance has never been the legal basis for sovereignty claims.
Secondly, after the UNCLOS came into practice, China had a claim of territorial sea and 【Thirdly】EEZ (exclusive economic zone) generated by UNCLOS based on the four island groups.
Finally, China has historic rights in the South China Sea.
Beijing has never used the nine-dash line to claim 90% of the South China Sea as China’s territory. That’s fake news. I also want to remind Mr. Ray Powell that you couldn’t claim the sea as your territories. We just claimed the four island groups as our territories, inheriting the claims from the Republic of China.
Also, the arbitration ruling has stated that all features in the South China Sea couldn’t generate 200 miles of EEZ. We should know that even during the negotiation of the UNCLOS, after 10 years of negotiations involving thousands of representatives from more than 100 countries, no agreement could be reached on what kind of features could generate 200 miles of EEZ. How can five arbitrators decide that? Who gave them the courage?
As to the historic rights, there are also two Chinese academic debates on that. In order to save time, I will not interpret that. You can see it in this screen.
The second misunderstanding is that China restricts foreign maritime activities in our EEZ, but we don’t have this kind of law. In practice, we just intercept when foreign maritime activities approach too much on our territorial sea or airspace.
The third misunderstanding is that China wants to change the status quo. The real reality is that China wants to keep the status quo.
I think even now Beijing follows Deng Xiaoping’s principle of shelving disputes . We recognize that the occupation state in the Spratly Islands happened in history, and we would not use force to return them back. But we couldn’t accept new losses.
The Second Thomas Shoal is not on the occupation list that Beijing recognized. I will talk about it later.
China has never fired the first shot. Many of you are talking about the water cannon, but you may not know that China has never fired even a single bullet to our neighbour for more than three decades. But the Philippines shot down Chinese Taiwan fishermen in 2013. Also, there have been open-fire incidents happening among ASEAN member states. For instance, Vietnamese fishermen have had very bloody conflicts with law enforcement forces of Malaysia and Indonesia in recent years.
So, in this regard, I think China’s performance is much better than that of other claimants. We also emphasize the stability in the neighborhood relationship with their neighbors. But China is also a sovereign state. When facing challenges to its sovereignty and maritime rights, China has a reason to respond and must respond.
Under the current administration of the Philippines, ever since late 2022 and up to now, I think the Philippines has protested against Beijing more than 500 times, demanding that all Chinese presence — all the personnel and vessels — should leave the West Philippine Sea. It’s a very ambitious demand.
There are also the new EDCA (Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement) sites, especially two of them pointing towards Taiwan, as well as the Philippines’ high-level officers saying that the Philippines has 250,000 Filipinos in Taiwan, so Taiwan’s contingency is the Philippines’ contingency. If Beijing uses the same logic, we can say that we have a lot of Chinese citizens in the Philippines and we have a lot of economic interests in the Philippines. So, the Philippines’ contingency is China’s contingency. So, I think this kind of thing is totally nonsense.
Also, the Philippines has proposed to extend its continental shelf beyond the 200 miles of the EEZ.
And there are two laws, which I think is very important, to trigger China’s response on the Scarborough Shoal.
The current Philippine administration, from the beginning, denied any kind of “gentleman’s agreement” with Beijing, but this kind of gentleman’s agreement existed even during the Aquino III administration.
And the Philippines has shown the intention to occupy all the features in the West Philippine Sea.
In the following part, we will review the cases one by one. The first case is the Second Thomas Shoal.
The Philippines grounded [a ship in] the Second Thomas Shoal in 1999. At the beginning, the Philippines told Beijing that they were just temporarily grounded. But they continued to ground it in this feature. Before 2022, Beijing and Manila had some understanding and a gentleman’s agreement that ordinary resupply is no problem but no building materials.
But when this administration came into office, they denied this kind of arrangement. Also, they wanted to challenge China’s bottom line on the Second Thomas Shoal. The amount of building materials transported was around 10 tonnes. Beijing waited a long time, almost a year, to persuade the Philippines to change its course. Beijing responded to the Philippines operation only in August 2023. We waited a long time.
But after the incident on June 17 , I think the Philippines realised that they should have some mutual understanding with Beijing. So we have another, we could say, gentleman’s agreement on the resupply.
So, generally, I think the situation of the Second Thomas Shoal is calming down compared with other features. One thing I should say is that the Second Thomas Shoal is different from Thitu Island and the other seven features the Philippines occupied. Beijing has never recognised the occupation state of the Second Thomas Shoal.
This is the Sabina Shoal. I think the confrontation just came out in this current administration.
The heated period is between April and September 2024. But finally, I think Beijing and the Philippines both know that neither has the intention to occupy this feature. There have been some incidents even this year, but generally I think the tensions around Sabina Shoal has been decreased.
Beijing has never recognised that there was dispute in the Scarborough Shoal. Beijing just recognised that there are disputes in the Spratly Islands. That’s Beijing’s position.
And in the Scarborough Shoal, the incident happened in 2012. During that incident, the Philippine naval officers tortured Chinese fishermen in the lagoon of the Scarborough Shoal. Beijing responded by sending law enforcement vessels there. After the incident, Beijing was worrying about that the Philippines might repeat this

articles.title_orig: Ukrainian Drones Set Russian Oil Infrastructure Ablaze in Twin Strikes Deep Inside Russia
articles.title_zh: Ukrainian Drones Set Russian Oil Infrastructure Ablaze in Twin Strikes Deep Inside Russia
articles.content_orig:
In brief: The reported strikes targeted the Kaleykino pumping station, a key hub for Russia’s Druzhba oil pipeline, and the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Products Plant. Both facilities play a role in Russia’s oil supply and export infrastructure.
Ukrainian drones struck two Russian oil facilities early on Monday, Nov. 23, sparking major fires at a pumping station in Tatarstan and an oil refinery in the Rostov region, according to local residents and Russian media reports.
In Tatarstan, residents reported explosions and a large fire near the Kaleykino oil pumping station outside Almetyevsk.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The facility, located around 1,300 kilometers (808 miles) from the Ukrainian border, is a key hub in Russia’s oil transportation network and the starting point of the Druzhba pipeline.
The independent Russian outlet Astra identified the burning facility as the Kaleykino station based on videos shared by eyewitnesses.
The site was targeted less than a week earlier, on Thursday, Nov. 19, when local authorities claimed a major fire had been avoided. Officials have not commented on the latest reported attack.
Kaleykino receives, stores, and pumps crude from oil fields across Tatarstan, Western Siberia, Udmurtia, and Bashkortostan.
It feeds oil into Russia’s network of trunk pipelines, including the Druzhba route, supplying refineries and supporting export flows.
Meanwhile, explosions and a major fire were reported at the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Products Plant in Russia’s Rostov region.
Astra reported , citing eyewitness footage, that the fire may have affected both the refinery and the nearby premises of TATA-GAZ LLC, a private company involved in fuel trading, storage, and logistics.
The Novoshakhtinsk plant is a major refinery in southern Russia, owned by Yug Energo LLC. It is connected to the Sukhodolnaya-Rodionovskaya oil pipeline and operates an oil loading terminal in Rostov-on-Don, as well as a fleet for transporting petroleum products.
Rostov Region Governor Yury Slyusar confirmed a fire caused by falling drone debris but did not identify the affected facility. He claimed that more than 80 drones had been shot down over the region overnight.
The strikes come amid an intensified Ukrainian campaign against Russia’s oil industry, targeting refineries, storage facilities, and pipeline infrastructure used to supply the military and generate revenue for Moscow’s war effort.
Ukrainian forces have struck at least nine Russian refineries since late October, including five of the country’s largest oil-processing plants, according to Ukraine’s General Staff.
The latest wave of attacks has repeatedly hit major facilities in southern Russia. On Wednesday, Nov. 18, Ukrainian drones struck the Afipsky and Ilsky refineries in Krasnodar Krai for the second time that month.
Earlier attacks also targeted Russia’s second-largest oil refinery near St. Petersburg and the Omsk refinery in Siberia , some 2,500 kilometers (1,553 miles) from Ukraine.
The sustained campaign has contributed to a roughly 30% decline in Russian crude processing and fuel shortages in several regions, according to Ukrainian officials and industry estimates.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

Wojtek Radwanski/Getty Images
Morning Brew delivers quick and insightful updates about the business world every day of the week from Wall St. to Silicon Valley.
The copper market is in disarray, and the penny was officially removed from production on Friday. Coincidence? Actually, yes. Copper’s recent downturn has more than numismatists worried, as analysts believe it signals that the job market, manufacturing, and the S&P 500 may be headed for declines.
That’s not a reference to gang activity in GTA VI . A death cross is a technical pattern in finance trends that can be “a warning sign for economic growth,” as Renaissance Macro put it. Currently, the Bloomberg Industrials Metal Index, which is 40% copper, is flashing one.
Since copper is used in home construction, auto manufacturing, and data center buildouts, that’s not a great sign:
On Friday, copper cost about $5.48 a pound, down from $6.89 in September.
Another driver of the falling prices , however, may be the (fading) spectre of new tariffs. There is currently no levy on raw copper being imported into the US. But President Trump’s repeated threats of enacting one since retaking office led companies to stockpile the metal stateside over the past two years:
No better than bullion: Gold prices are also down, and the AI stock sell-off is partly to blame. Not every investor is selling out at a profit—some are cutting their losses , and when they do, Fast Company said, they tend to liquidate assets like gold to cover them.— HVL

articles.title_orig: China Fears A.I. Could Give the U.S. an Edge in Nuclear Rivalry
articles.title_zh: China Fears A.I. Could Give the U.S. an Edge in Nuclear Rivalry
articles.content_orig:
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with China's President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit on Nov. 19, 2026.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is placing particular focus on renewing relations with China as he aims to deepen international trade ties and diversify from U.S. reliance amid a three-month-long trade war with the U.S.
When asked what cards Canada holds in its ongoing talks with Washington, Carney, who recently announced a new partnership with the E.U. , pointed to the country's budding relationships elsewhere.
“Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said Wednesday during a remote interview with the New York Times from Shenzhen, China, where he was among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit . "If the U.S. doesn't want to do the deal, we're busy.” His remarks came in the wake of President Donald Trump's claim that the U.S. holds “all the cards” after trade talks collapsed in August, leading to both sides enforcing heavy retaliatory tariffs .
Carney and Trump had a meeting on the sidelines of APEC, but aside from a commitment to “continue” negotiations and stay in close contact, no progress was made. However, Carney painted his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in a much more positive light. Ahead of the summit, Carney and Xi announced a Canada-China trade pact , which provided additional tariff relief on Canadian food and agricultural exports into China, and in return saw Canada agree to extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years.
Carney, who is promoting a “Canada Strong” platform as he aims to build economic resilience at home, touted the expansion of the trade arrangement with China as something that will deliver “greater certainty and prosperity for all Canadians.” He also praised the negotiation process with China, saying: “They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”
In an eight-day tour that took him from a European summit in Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia, and finally China for the APEC gathering, Carney forged ahead with his plan to diversify Canada's economy away from its dependence on the U.S., which by far remains the country's largest trading partner .
Experts say Canada's progress in deepening its economic relationships with China could challenge Trump's insistence that Washington holds the upper hand in trade negotiations.
“Part of the Trump Administration’s [belief] is that everybody needs the U.S. more than anything else, and therefore the U.S. has maximum leverage,” says Jennifer Hillman, co-director of the Institute of International Economic Law at Georgetown University. “What this is clearly saying is that Canada can afford to be less willing to give the U.S. whatever it asks for [in negotiations], because they have other options.”
China has the world's second-largest economy , behind only the U.S., giving it the potential to become a much larger market for Canadian goods than some of the other countries Carney has sought to deepen relations with.
“China represents a very big market and the potential of a really big trading partner,” says Lori Turnbull, a professor in the Faculty of Management at Dalhousie University, noting it could be a leverage point in U.S. negotiations. “Doing a deal with a country like China is something that [the U.S.] will care about because of the size of China's economy and its competitive relationship with the U.S.”
Carney's latest push to strengthen trade ties with Beijing forms part of a months-long effort to renew Canada-China relations. In January, he met with Xi to forge what he called a “ new strategic partnership ,” agreeing to allow in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a tariff of 6.1%, rather than the previous 100% levy. China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
The move drew criticism from Trump, who said that “China will eat Canada alive, completely devour it, including the destruction of their businesses, social fabric, and general way of life.”
While Canada's closer relationship with China could strengthen its hand in negotiations, experts also warn that it could backfire.
Turnbull points to the latest agreement to extend tariff exemptions on Chinese steel and aluminum as a potential source of tension with Washington. “Things like reducing tariffs on select steel and aluminum products coming from China is something that might make the U.S. and not just Donald Trump, but also [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer angry,” she suggests.
Steel, aluminum, and auto tariffs were among the major points of contention when U.S.-Canada trade negotiations broke down in August, with both sides accusing each other of walking back commitments.
Carney, however, has played down concerns that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is a major issue for Trump.
“In my conversation with the President, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China,” said Carney during a news conference in Shenzhen. “I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all.”
Meanwhile, some Canadian officials have voiced concerns on expanding trade with China.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned Carney on Monday against opening the door for more Chinese-made EV vehicles in Canada, arguing the “government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars.”
Michael Chong, a lawmaker from Canada’s Conservative Party, during a press conference on Wednesday supported maintaining a dialogue with Beijing, but described Carney’s budding strategic partnership with China as a “risky gambit,” citing potential “national security” concerns.
In 2025, Ottawa identified China as one of the main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage against Canada alongside other countries such as Russia and Iran. The Canadian government’s own analysis of Canada-China relations also points out that there are "associated risks” in broader trade cooperation in key areas, such as “prevalent and persistent intellectual property theft, and the risk of diversion of sensitive goods and technologies intended for civilian use for military purposes and applications.”
Carney said ahead of his Asia trip that he would raise concerns about foreign interference in his meeting with Xi. "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” he told reporters in Montreal on Nov. 10. Carney added that he would stress the importance Canada places on "the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”
In a press briefing during the APEC summit, Carney emphasized that Canada's trade with China is largely focused on commodities, rather than sensitive technologies such as advanced semiconductors.
“We are exporting canola, we are exporting pork. We are exporting halibut,” Carney said , also citing liquefied natural gas and oil. “These are important industries. These are not cutting-edge semi-conductors.”
Experts point out that Canada could pursue deeper cooperation with other international partners in sectors where a closer relationship with China would be more difficult, including defense and advanced technology.
“[Canada] is not going to partner with China on defense, security, AI, and digital technology, things like that would be very difficult. [Carney] would have an impossible time trying to convince Canadians that's what we should be doing,” says Turnbull. “For those things, [Canada] would be putting [its] arms around the European Union.”
In September, the European Union unveiled its vision for Canada to become an “associate member” of the bloc. During an E.U.-Canada summit in Montreal in October, the two sides underscored their commitment to this plan, paving the way for deeper cooperation in areas including A

articles.title_orig: Electrification 'distraction' failed: Richard Denniss on COP31 collapse
articles.title_zh: Electrification 'distraction' failed: Richard Denniss on COP31 collapse
articles.content_orig:
The COP31 summit in Turkey came as evidence of climate change could not have been clearer - 2026 bought glacier collapses, record European heat, and wildfires across Asia - but also when geopolitical divisions could not have been deeper.
The result was the longest-running climate talks in UN history failed to deliver on its central political agreement â the Antalya Pacts - to further climate action.
Despite two countries, Australia and Turkey, leading the charge in their joint hosting of the negotiations, they could not bring the nations together.
After a dramatic and fractious final day where countries walked out over the absence of mention of fossil fuels in the text and money issues, questions are being asked more loudly than ever before about whether the COP process can still deliver.
Here are five, key takeaways from the talks which the hosts hoped would become known as the "implementation COP".
This was the first COP since the UN warned that global temperatures are expected to exceed 1.5C degrees above pre-industrial levels. That is the threshold which countries agreed not to breach as part of the Paris Climate Agreement signed in 2015.
The draft agreement had acknowledged the uncomfortable reality that climate action to date has failed on its most crucial of targets.
Without agreement, that recognition has been lost.
Almost exactly a decade ago a group of the world's climate scientists - the official UN body the IPCC - warned what would happen if temperatures rose 1.5C vs 2C:
Sea level rise would be 10cm higher - that would expose 10 million more people to flooding , external
The ocean would become more acidic risking irreversible damage to some marine life
Extreme heat - that's hot days and nights - in every inhabited part of the world
In a 2C world extreme heat is expected to be experienced in every inhabitated area on Earth
Throughout the talks and during the final day, many countries still acknowledged that the target remained their north star of climate action.
"This COP sought to confront hard truths â that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with even more urgency to reduce emissions," said UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh at the close of the talks.
The draft had called for that overshoot to be kept as small and short-lived as possible â it also suggested something called carbon dioxide removal (CDR).
This is a process which takes greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere and has not been explicitly mentioned in a COP final agreement before.
Carbon dioxide can be removed naturally by planting trees - although there are limits to the scale and permanence of that.
There are other technological solutions, but these are controversial , external and are not well advanced.
This year's negotiations have exposed a troubling problem - consensus does not last forever.
On the central political agreement â the Antalya Pacts â countries could not bridge the divide on including language on fossil fuels.
And yet the very same pledge had been made just three years ago at COP28 in Dubai.
Rich nations also failed to put a figure to how much more money could be given to developing countries to adapt to climate change.
This is despite there already being a commitment from last year to triple the figure by 2035 from $40bn (Â£30bn) - but the interpretation of that pledge remains contested.
If governments cannot even agree to reaffirm commitments they've already made, it raises troubling questions about their ability to work together as the climate crisis intensifies.
Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed
Minister Chris Bowen from Australia, who was co-leading the negotiations, pointed out at the end of the talks that the world is a very different place from when these commitments were struck just a few years ago.
"The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory".
That was made apparent during the final meeting when pointed remarks were delivered. EU representative Darragh O'Brien said the talks had been "hijacked by some oil states".
Russian delegate Sergei Kononuchenko switched from Russian to English to directly address the EU delegation. He accused them of providing climate finance only in the form of loans to developing nations: "This is an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner".
It is a serious blow not just to climate action, but to multilateralism itself - the idea that countries can put aside their differences on other issues to tackle problems they can't solve alone.
Much of the coverage of COP31 has focused on the failure to get the central political agreement passed.
But much of the work at these summits is putting into action agreements made at previous meetings.
On money that is going towards adaptation for example, countries need to agree how is it being distributed, is it making an impact and how can this be tracked, and which areas are particularly vulnerable.
In fact, there were 164 other items on this year's agenda that were being thrashed out in the negotiating rooms.
And some of those were agreed at the talks.
The funds raised from a global system of carbon credits â money given in exchange for releasing greenhouse gases â will go towards helping developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change.
They agreed to advance a just transition framework designed to protect workers and communities as global economies shift toward clean energy.
But there were many more that could not be agreed and some will now be picked up at COP32, including crucially the work programme responsible for driving forward action on cutting emissions.
What governments agree in the COP negotiating rooms is only part of what determines the speed of the energy transition.
The International Energy Agency's latest World Energy Outlook , external points to another powerful force: energy security.
It says the disruption to oil and gas supplies through the Strait of Hormuz has been the biggest energy supply shock in history. The longer the uncertainty continues, the stronger the incentive for countries to switch from imported fossil fuels to electricity generated at home.
Renewable energy capacity is expected to grow 60% more over the next six-year period than the previous
The economics have been changing too.
Solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles have become increasingly competitive.
As clean energy develops its own commercial momentum, formal negotiations may become less important in determining its direction and pace.
Against the headwinds of inflation new investment announcements emerged at COP as part of the "Action Agenda".
This is the part of the COP process that tries to mobilise action outside of formal talks from businesses, investors and cities â this year the focus was on electrification. Turning more of our energy from fossil fuels to electricity.
"We are not entering the age of electricity, we have arrived at the age of electricity," Fatih Birol, head of the IEA, told the BBC. He says energy security and climate policies are now "closely aligned".
That doesn't make COP irrelevant.
Governments still have a crucial role in facilitating the transition, according to Dr Jennie Dodson, a senior director at the World Business Council for Sustainable Development which includes among its members the likes of Amazon and Apple.
"A key message from business is we can go so far, a lot of it is cost competitive, but there are policy barriers both around infrastructure and permitting".
Many are questioning whether the COP process is fit for purpose
COP31 has shown how the role of these annual UN climate conferences is changing.
For the first 30 COPs, the emphasis was on building the international framework for tackling global warming.
The great diplomatic breakthrough came in Paris in 2015, when almost every country agreed to keep global warming well below 2Â°C and to pursue efforts to limit it to

articles.content_orig:
Reactions to ICJ ruling underline global divisions over court with China raising concerns about judicial overreach
The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.
Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel .
The EU hailed a “landmark” judgment from the ICJ, while the UK reaffirmed “full support” for the court and the international legal order. Australia called on Myanmar to comply fully with the judgment and its obligations under international law.
But China, which has offered rare international support for Myanmar’s military rulers since they seized power five years ago, highlighted “issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation”.
“China … believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told a news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue.”
Western nations cut ties with the unstable and poor south-east Asian country after the 2021 coup that ousted a civilian-led government.
Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson said on Friday that the ruling was “unfair”, noting the judges’ nine to six vote. The country’s military rulers have denied carrying out a genocide, claiming their actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted insurgent attacks.
“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” said Khaing Khaing Soe, speaking at a press conference in the capital, Naypyidaw. “So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair.”
The US state department said on Thursday that Washington was examining the judgment, while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.
Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), but has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.
The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”, noting that the US was the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.
In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.
“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement .
“The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”.
The UK expelled Myanmar’s defence attache and called for measures to “ensure the court’s ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity”.
The ruling caps a lengthy legal campaign since August 2017 when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. Reports rapidly emerged of mass rapes and killings by security forces, as well as the burning of thousands of homes.
Judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.
The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the ICC – which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states – on allegations of crimes against humanity.
The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited .
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across the Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia . Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

articles.title_orig: China Finds Another Route to Protein -This Time From Industrial Gas
articles.title_zh: China Finds Another Route to Protein -This Time From Industrial Gas
articles.content_orig:
China's search for new ways to produce protein is taking another interesting turn. Researchers at the Tianjin Institute of Industrial Biotechnology are investigating how industrial gases can be converted into nutrients for microorganisms capable of producing protein. It's another indication China isn't betting on a single technology to strengthen its future food supply.
The process begins with syngas — a mixture of gases that can be generated from industrial processes or biomass. Through fermentation, microorganisms convert these gases into compounds including acetate, which can then feed a second fermentation process. Chinese researchers have been testing how this nutrient-rich liquid can support the growth of Yarrowia lipolytica , a yeast with potential applications in microbial protein production.
The early results are encouraging. Researchers reported a 7.7% improvement in yeast biomass production in a five-litre fermenter, alongside an increase in acetate conversion from 21.68% to 41.1%. These are laboratory-scale results, not evidence that commercially competitive food protein is about to reach supermarket shelves. Nevertheless, they demonstrate another possible route towards producing useful biomass without relying exclusively on conventional crops or livestock.
What makes this particularly interesting is the wider Chinese strategy. From precision fermentation and cultivated proteins to microbial biomass and alternative fermentation feedstocks, Chinese researchers are exploring multiple approaches to protein production. Each has different technical and economic challenges, but collectively they could expand the country's future production options.
For countries such as New Zealand, the question is worth asking: if protein can increasingly be produced using industrial carbon streams, microorganisms and controlled fermentation systems, how might that change the economics of food production and national food security? China appears determined to find out.
